paras: The Racine street laborers' fight was a brawl on August 9, 1895, in Racine, Wisconsin, in which a discharged white laborer attacked the Black foreman of a city street crew and white men and Black laborers then fought on a principal street. Police ended the fight, and the foreman, Lockhardt, was the only man reported arrested. Wisconsin papers printed the story under the headline "Race War at Racine."

Contractor Jones had recently brought Lockhardt, described as "a colored man from Milwaukee," to supervise street work in Racine. According to the report, people living near the work site had complained about how he treated the laborers, and the dispatch called him "a very tyrannical sort of a fellow."

On the morning of August 9, Lockhardt discharged a laborer named George Sherry, who refused to stop working until he was paid. Lockhardt told him to collect his wages from the contractor. Shortly afterward, as Lockhardt walked along the street, Sherry attacked him, and in the general fight that followed "the white man got the worst of it."

White men nearby then took Sherry's side, and the whole crew of Black laborers joined Lockhardt, so that there was "a fight on all sides for a time." The dispatch said the Black laborers had the better of it because they outnumbered their opponents, and that the crowd dispersed when police arrived. No injuries are described in detail.

Lockhardt was arrested and jailed, then released on bonds; no arrest of Sherry or of the white men is reported. The dispatch closed by warning that "more trouble is threatened, as the white men are thoroughly aroused." No report of a hearing, a trial, or further violence appears in the coverage.

The only account is a special dispatch from Racine dated August 9, which the Watertown Republican printed on August 14. The Eagle River Review ran the same text a day later without the dateline. Both papers used the headline "Race War at Racine" with the subhead "Objected to a Colored Boss," and the dispatch called the fight "nothing less than a race war" in which "the whites were pitted against the blacks."

Although the dispatch said Sherry began the attack, it opened with neighbors' complaints about Lockhardt's conduct and ended with the warning about aroused white men, without quoting Lockhardt or any of the Black laborers. No coverage of the fight in the Black press or in a Racine paper was found.

accounts.label: Racine special (wire)
accounts.gist: Lockhardt, described as tyrannical, discharged Sherry, who later attacked him; white men took Sherry's side, the colored laborers took Lockhardt's, and the colored men, being the majority, had the better of it until police came. Lockhardt alone is reported arrested.

framing.detail: The special said Sherry attacked Lockhardt, yet headlined the fight as a 'Race War' over a 'Colored Boss', described Lockhardt as 'tyrannical' on the word of neighbors, and closed by warning that 'the white men are thoroughly aroused'.
The Eagle River Review ran the same text and headline a day later without the dateline.
